payload.root_cause: Inventory.snapshot() does not copy the internal stock dict. At pyshop/inventory.py:36 it does `snapshot = self._stock` (binding a reference to the internal dict) and returns it, so the returned object IS self._stock. Any caller mutating the 'snapshot' mutates the real stock levels, contradicting the method's own docstring ('Return a copy ... callers may mutate it freely'). Note the contrast with __init__ (line 10), which defensively copies input with `dict(stock or {})`. The fix belongs in snapshot(): return a copy (e.g., dict comprehension of available quantities per sku).

payload.rationale: The root cause is that Inventory.snapshot() returns the internal self._stock dict by reference (`snapshot = self._stock return snapshot`), so any caller mutating the returned dict mutates the real stock levels, contradicting the docstring's promise of a freely mutable copy. Replacing the aliased reference with `return dict(self._stock)` makes a shallow copy of the internal stock dict (values are ints, immutable, so a shallow copy suffices), matching the codebase's existing defensive-copy convention seen in __init__ (`dict(stock or {})`). Mutating the snapshot no longer affects self._stock, so available() reports correct stock. This is the minimal change: it only fixes the aliasing without altering snapshot's existing semantics of exposing the stock mapping.
